blocks.text: 1. Enterprise Search

blocks.alt: Many heterogeneous sources feed a unified index powering a search interface

blocks.text: Chat with PDFs closed by pointing toward enterprise search as the better fit for a shared, permanent knowledge base. Enterprise Search, a RAG system design for finding answers across an organization's entire shared knowledge base, is exactly that system, scaled up from one user's documents to an entire company.
It indexes a large, continuously changing document collection and enforces per-user permissions on every result.
2. The Design Problem's Scope
Unlike Chat with PDFs, this system serves an entire organization from one shared, permanent index.
Documents come from many sources and many different teams, not one user's upload.

blocks.text: 3. Ingesting From Many Heterogeneous Sources

blocks.alt: Wiki, Slack, and Drive are all ingested into one system

blocks.text: Following the batch versus API ingestion approaches covered in Document Ingestion, wikis, tickets, chat logs, and internal documents each need their own ingestion pipeline feeding one shared index.
A single unified chunk schema lets retrieval treat all these different sources consistently.
4. Permission-Aware Retrieval Is Non-Negotiable

blocks.alt: A query goes through a permission filter to produce allowed results only

blocks.text: As with the access control at the retrieval level covered in Security, a search result the requesting user is not permitted to see must never appear at all.
Every chunk carries permission metadata, checked before ranking.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A confidential HR document accidentally surfacing in a general employee's search results would be a serious failure, exactly why permission checks at retrieval time are treated as non-negotiable in enterprise search.

blocks.text: 5. Hybrid Search Across Diverse Document Types

blocks.alt: Semantic search and keyword search combine into hybrid results

blocks.text: As covered under hybrid search in Retrieval, a precise ticket number needs keyword matching, while a vague conceptual question needs semantic search.
Combining both retrieval styles serves the full range of how employees actually search.

blocks.text: 6. Keeping The Index Current As Documents Change Constantly

blocks.alt: A document change triggers an incremental update

blocks.text: As Real-Time Updates covers, an internal wiki page or ticket changes constantly across a large organization.
Incremental indexing keeps the shared index from silently going stale.
7. Cross-Team Results Require Consistent Metadata Standards

blocks.alt: Team A metadata and team B metadata follow the same standard

blocks.text: As with the knowledge graphs versus relational tables comparison in Knowledge Graphs, different teams tag their own content inconsistently unless a shared metadata standard is actually enforced.
Without that standard, cross-team search results become unreliable.
8. Scale To A Huge And Growing Corpus
As Scaling Strategies covers with horizontal versus vertical scaling, a large enterprise's document corpus can grow into millions of chunks over time.
The vector index itself needs its own dedicated scaling plan, separate from the app layer.
9. Recognizing When This Enterprise Search Design Fits The Actual Need

blocks.alt: Many sources needing unified search points toward this enterprise search design

blocks.text: A large organization searching its own shared internal knowledge fits this design.
One user's own uploaded documents fits chat with PDFs better instead.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates permission-filtered hybrid search across heterogeneous document types with consistent metadata.

code.content:
documents = [
    {"id": "wiki1", "type": "wiki", "text": "Onboarding process for new engineers.", "allowed_roles": ["all"]},
    {"id": "ticket1", "type": "ticket", "text": "TICKET-4521: Login page returns 500 error.", "allowed_roles": ["all"]},
    {"id": "hr1", "type": "hr_doc", "text": "Salary bands for senior engineering roles.", "allowed_roles": ["hr", "admin"]},
]

def keyword_search(query, docs):
    # keyword matching handles precise terms
    return [d for d in docs if query.upper() in d["text"].upper()]

def semantic_search(query, docs):
    # semantic matching handles conceptual overlap
    return [d for d in docs if any(w in d["text"].lower() for w in query.lower().split())]

def permission_filter(results, user_role):
    # permission check applied before results are returned
    return [d for d in results if user_role in d["allowed_roles"] or "all" in d["allowed_roles"]]

def enterprise_search(query, user_role):
    keyword_hits = keyword_search(query, documents)
    semantic_hits = semantic_search(query, documents)
    combined = {d["id"]: d for d in keyword_hits + semantic_hits}.values()
    return permission_filter(combined, user_role)

print("Search results for 'employee' role:")
for d in enterprise_search("onboarding engineer", "employee"):
    print(f"  [{d['type']}] {d['id']}: {d['text']}")

print("\nSearch for salary info as 'employee' role (should be filtered out):")
print([d["id"] for d in enterprise_search("salary bands", "employee")])

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the salary document correctly filtered out for the employee role while onboarding and ticket results remain visible.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Building one retrieval path for all document types instead of combining keyword and semantic search.
Skipping permission checks at retrieval time, risking confidential documents surfacing broadly.
Letting each team tag its own content with inconsistent metadata standards.
Underestimating how much the vector index itself needs its own dedicated scaling plan at enterprise scale.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Enterprise search finds answers across an organization's entire shared, permanent knowledge base.
Unlike chat with PDFs, it serves an entire organization from one shared index, not one user's uploads.
Wikis, tickets, chat logs, and documents each need their own ingestion pipeline feeding one shared index.
Permission checks at retrieval time are non-negotiable; a disallowed result must never appear at all.
Combining keyword and semantic search serves both precise IDs and vague conceptual questions.
Incremental indexing keeps the shared index from going stale as documents change constantly.
A consistent, enforced metadata standard keeps cross-team search results reliable.
The vector index needs its own dedicated scaling plan as the corpus grows into millions of chunks.
